title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) on SKU Deletion
description:
The SKU deletion endpoint (sku_delete.php) is vulnerable to Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks. The endpoint lacks CSRF protection mechanisms such as CSRF tokens or same-site cookie policies. An attacker can craft a malicious webpage that, when visited by a user, will silently delete arbitrary SKU records without the user's knowledge or consent. The deletion request succeeds regardless of the Origin or Referer headers, confirming no CSRF validation is performed on state-changing operations.

The vulnerability was confirmed by sending a POST request with cross-origin headers (Origin: http://evil.com, Referer: http://evil.com) to the sku_delete.php endpoint. The server accepted and processed the request without any CSRF token validation or cross-origin restrictions, returning HTTP 302 (redirect) to indicate successful processing.
impact: An attacker can trick users (particularly administrators) into visiting a malicious website, which would then silently delete SKU records from the target system via CSRF attacks. This could result in data destruction and business disruption without user awareness. When combined with the IDOR vulnerability, this allows attackers to delete any arbitrary SKU record via CSRF. An attacker could exploit this by creating a malicious page with hidden requests that trigger deletion when visited by an authenticated user.
evidence:
POC Execution Output:
- HTTP Response Code: 302 (Redirect) - Server accepted cross-origin request
- Cross-origin headers were not rejected: Origin: http://evil.com, Referer: http://evil.com
- No CSRF token validation: Request succeeded without any token parameter
- Request payload: POST data with id=10
- Vulnerability confirmed: Cross-origin deletion requests are processed by the server

The server's acceptance of the cross-origin request (HTTP 302 response) indicates that no CSRF protection is in place. A properly secured application would reject or require validation for state-changing requests from different origins.
remediation:
1. Implement CSRF token validation: Generate cryptographically secure CSRF tokens for each user session and require their submission with all state-changing requests (POST, PUT, DELETE).

2. Implement SameSite cookie attribute: Set the SameSite attribute on session cookies to "Strict" or "Lax" to prevent cross-site cookie transmission.

3. Validate Origin and Referer headers: Check that requests originate from trusted domains and reject requests from unauthorized origins.

4. Use the Double Submit Cookie pattern: Generate and verify unique tokens that are both sent as cookies and request parameters.

5. Implement CSRF middleware: Use framework-provided CSRF protection middleware or security libraries to automatically validate tokens.

6. Add security headers: Implement X-CSRF-Token header validation for API endpoints.

7. Consider API token authentication: For API endpoints, use token-based authentication instead of session-based auth to provide additional CSRF protection.
